ana_01.title: Champion odds — Argentina 30.8% leads a steep ladder
ana_01.claim: As of the 2026-06-23 snapshot, the model gives Argentina the best chance of lifting the trophy at 30.8%, ahead of Spain (24.0%), France (14.2%), England (8.0%), Colombia (4.8%) and Brazil (3.3%). The distribution is steep and top-heavy: the top two account for more than half of all title probability, and only 13 of the 48 teams have even a 1% chance. These are championship probabilities — the share of 100,000 simulated tournaments each team wins — and they sum to 1.000 across the field. Argentina leads not because it is guaranteed anything, but because across every plausible bracket it survives more often than anyone else.

ana_02.title: Where the model fights the FIFA ranking
ana_02.claim: A results-trained Elo model re-orders the official FIFA ladder, and among the 13 real contenders the disagreements are sharp. The model's biggest upgrade is Norway, ranked 31st by FIFA but lifted to the 10th-best title chance (1.8%); next is Colombia, FIFA's 13th but the model's 5th pick at 4.8%, then Japan (FIFA 18th up to 12th) and Germany (10th up to 7th). In the other direction the model fades market darlings: Portugal drops from FIFA 5th to 9th and Morocco from 7th to 11th. At the very top the two systems agree — Argentina, Spain, France and England are 1-2-3-4 on both. Where they part ways is where a reader has the most room to argue.

ana_03.title: Money vs. merit — Colombia is five times cheaper than France

France carries the costliest squad in the tournament at €1.52bn and the model gives it a 45.5% chance of reaching the semi-finals — €33m of squad value per percentage point of that chance. Colombia's squad costs €302m, roughly a fifth of France's, yet the model still gives it a 22.1% semi-final chance, at just €14m per point — more than twice as efficient. ana_04.title: The bracket is a coin-flip for three teams
ana_04.claim: Because only the top two of each group advance automatically and the eight best third-placed teams fill the rest of the new Round of 32, qualification splits the field into two worlds. Sixteen teams are already all but through (reach-R32 probability of 99% or more): Argentina, Spain, France, Brazil, Germany and others. But three teams sit on a true knife edge, with a reach-R32 probability between 40% and 60% — Senegal (55.1%), Bosnia & Herzegovina (47.9%) and DR Congo (47.1%) — for whom a single result swings the whole tournament. For those three, the model isn't predicting so much as measuring a coin toss.

ana_06.title: Why believe it — beats a naive baseline on 8,000 games, edges it on these 44
ana_06.claim: The forecast earns trust by being checked, and the check is reported honestly. On a large out-of-sample test of 8,000 historical internationals the model clearly beats a naive baseline (which just predicts the home/draw/away base rates): log-loss 0.892 versus 1.061 — about 16% lower error — and 59.4% result accuracy versus 48.7%. That is the reliable read. On the 44 games of THIS World Cup already played, the model edges the naive baseline too (log-loss 0.969 vs 1.067; accuracy 56.8% vs 52.3%), but a 44-game sample is small and upset-prone, so it neither confirms nor refutes the model on its own. The honest summary: a clear, replicable edge on the large sample; a slim, noisy edge on the games played so far.

ana_07.title: Who you'd play is itself a distribution — 495 of them
ana_07.claim: Even for a team that is certain to advance, the model cannot name its Round-of-32 opponent yet, because the pairings depend on which eight of the twelve third-placed teams qualify. FIFA's Annex C tabulates all C(12,8) = 495 of those combinations, and the simulation integrates over every one. Argentina, for example, reaches the Round of 32 in essentially 100% of simulations, but the team it meets there is spread across many possible opponents — a distribution, not a fixture. This is the structural reason a mid-tournament forecast for the first 48-team World Cup has to be probabilistic about the bracket, not just the winner.

det_01.title: The first 48-team World Cup and its new Round of 32
det_01.claim: 2026 is the first FIFA World Cup with 48 teams instead of 32, split into 12 groups of four. The two group winners and runners-up advance automatically, and the eight best third-placed teams fill the rest of a brand-new 32-team knockout round (the Round of 32) that did not exist in any previous men's World Cup. That single format change is why a mid-tournament forecast is unusually hard: with 12 third places competing for 8 slots and the bracket keyed to which specific groups those eight come from, the knockout pairings are not fixed until the group stage ends. The tournament is hosted across the United States, Canada and Mexico and runs to a 2026-07-19 final.

det_02.title: Why the bracket is a distribution, not a diagram (FIFA Annex C)
det_02.claim: FIFA Regulations Annex C specifies, in advance, exactly which Round-of-32 slot each qualifying third-placed team fills — but the assignment depends on WHICH eight of the twelve groups produce a qualifying third. There are C(12,8) = 495 such combinations, and Annex C is literally a 495-row lookup table. Until the final group standings are known, 'who you'd play in the Round of 32' is therefore itself a probability distribution over those 495 permutations rather than a single pairing. A forecast made at the second-matchday snapshot must integrate over all of them, which is precisely what a Monte-Carlo simulation does naturally.

det_03.title: Elo + Poisson + Monte-Carlo: a standard, transparent forecasting recipe
det_03.claim: The forecast uses a well-established three-step recipe rather than a proprietary black box. First, an Elo rating is fit on roughly a century and a half of international results (martj42's ~49k matches since 1872), giving each of the 48 teams a single strength number as of the snapshot. Second, the Elo difference between two teams is converted into expected goals via a Poisson goal model calibrated on post-2002 internationals. Third, a Monte-Carlo simulation plays out every remaining match and the full bracket tens of thousands of times, and the share of simulations a team wins becomes its championship probability. Elo-based football models in this family (FiveThirtyEight's Soccer Power Index, Eloratings.net) are the public benchmark for this kind of forecast, which is why the method earns reader trust only if it can be checked against what already happened.

det_04.title: Leakage guard — a live mirror that already knows the future
det_04.claim: The historical results file is a live mirror that already contains the 2026 World Cup matches played after the pre-tournament cutoff, including the group games used as an out-of-sample check. A naive model that trained on the whole file would secretly learn the very results it is meant to forecast — a textbook data-leakage failure. The honest discipline is to fit ratings only on matches dated before the 2026-06-23 forecast frontier (and to score the already-played World Cup games from the leak-free pre-tournament Elo), so the model never trains on a game it is supposed to predict; the post-cutoff rows are reserved as an out-of-sample check, never as training input. Stating this guard openly is part of why the resulting numbers can be trusted.

det_05.title: Money vs. merit — the most expensive squads rarely win
det_05.claim: Squad market value (Transfermarkt) and on-pitch strength are correlated but far from identical, and World Cup history is full of expensive squads that fell short and cheaper ones that overran them. The contrast is a recurring data-journalism hook: a forecast driven by results-based Elo will systematically disagree with a ranking driven by transfer-market wages, flagging which squads the market over- or under-values relative to their simulated chance of a deep run. In this dataset France and England carry the costliest squads (well over €1bn each), yet a results-based model can still rank a cheaper side ahead of them.

France carries the costliest squad in the tournament at €1.52bn and the model gives it a 45.5% chance of reaching the semi-finals — €33m of squad value per percentage point of that chance. Colombia's squad costs €302m, roughly a fifth of France's, yet the model still gives it a 22.1% semi-final chance, at just €14m per point — more than twice as efficient. The clearest bargains are Argentina (€12m per semi-final point) and Colombia; the most expensive by this measure are Portugal (€80m per point) and Germany (€56m). des_predictor.title: des_predictor
des_predictor.claim: As of the 2026-06-23 snapshot, the model gives Argentina the best chance of lifting the trophy at 30.8%, ahead of Spain (24.0%), France (14.2%), England (8.0%), Colombia (4.8%) and Brazil (3.3%). The distribution is steep and top-heavy: the top two account for more than half of all title probability, and only 13 of the 48 teams have even a 1% chance. These are championship probabilities — the share of 100,000 simulated tournaments each team wins — and they sum to 1.000 across the field. Argentina leads not because it is guaranteed anything, but because across every plausible bracket it survives more often than anyone else.

des_rankgap_chart.title: Model vs FIFA rank — diverging bar
des_rankgap_chart.claim: A results-trained Elo model re-orders the official FIFA ladder, and among the 13 real contenders the disagreements are sharp. The model's biggest upgrade is Norway, ranked 31st by FIFA but lifted to the 10th-best title chance (1.8%); next is Colombia, FIFA's 13th but the model's 5th pick at 4.8%, then Japan (FIFA 18th up to 12th) and Germany (10th up to 7th). In the other direction the model fades market darlings: Portugal drops from FIFA 5th to 9th and Morocco from 7th to 11th. At the very top the two systems agree — Argentina, Spain, France and England are 1-2-3-4 on both. Where they part ways is where a reader has the most room to argue.

# --- ana_02: FIFA ranking vs model ranking — disagreements among real contenders ---
print("\n=== ana_02 ===")
d = champ.copy()
d["model_rank"] = d["p_champion"].rank(ascending=False, method="min").astype(int)
d["rank_gap"] = d["fifa_rank"] - d["model_rank"]   # positive = model likes it MORE than FIFA
# restrict to teams the model gives a non-trivial title chance (>=1%) so the disagreement is meaningful,

liked = contenders.sort_values("rank_gap", ascending=False).head(5)
faded = contenders.sort_values("rank_gap").head(5)

des_stars_chart.title: Stars vs deep run — EA overall against team reach-semifinal odds
des_stars_chart.claim: As of the 2026-06-23 snapshot, the model gives Argentina the best chance of lifting the trophy at 30.8%, ahead of Spain (24.0%), France (14.2%), England (8.0%), Colombia (4.8%) and Brazil (3.3%). The distribution is steep and top-heavy: the top two account for more than half of all title probability, and only 13 of the 48 teams have even a 1% chance. These are championship probabilities — the share of 100,000 simulated tournaments each team wins — and they sum to 1.000 across the field. Argentina leads not because it is guaranteed anything, but because across every plausible bracket it survives more often than anyone else.
des_stars_chart.code:
# This scatter joins two sources, one point per player:
#   x = player EA overall -> EA Sports FC rating (CITED, not computed here; frozen in code/ea_ratings.json)
#   y = team p_reach_sf   -> the Monte-Carlo forecast (code/simulate.py, cell_simulate; forecast_outputs/advance_probs.csv)
# merged on each player's national team. The loose vertical scatter at high EA overall is the 'stars != deep run' point.
# Only the y-axis and the join are ours; the x-axis values are EA's published ratings.
des_stars_chart.expected_output:
Argentina      grp J  FIFA# 1  Elo 2220  champ  30.8%  reach-final  48.1%
Spain          grp H  FIFA# 2  Elo 2198  champ  24.0%  reach-final  40.6%
France         grp I  FIFA# 3  Elo 2154  champ  14.2%  reach-final  26.2%
England        grp L  FIFA# 4  Elo 2121  champ   8.0%  reach-final  16.1%
Colombia       grp K  FIFA#13  Elo 2082  champ   4.8%  reach-final  11.1%
Brazil         grp C  FIFA# 6  Elo 2073  champ   3.3%  reach-final   7.8%
top1 Argentina = 30.8%
champion prob sums to 1.000 over 48 teams
teams with >=1% champ chance: 13

run.note: x-axis (EA overall) is a cited EA Sports FC value (code/ea_ratings.json), not reproduced here; y-axis (team reach-semifinal odds) is reproducible offline via the Monte-Carlo (cell_simulate -> forecast_outputs/advance_probs.csv).

des_stars_chart._note: Hybrid provenance: the x-axis is cited EA Sports FC overall (code/ea_ratings.json), the y-axis is this project's Monte-Carlo reach-semifinal odds (code/simulate.py). The element is tagged data-ana=ana_07 on the page but it is NOT the bracket finding -- it overlays EA ratings with model reach-SF odds.

ana_histbase.title: Is 30.8% a lot? Only eight nations have ever won
ana_histbase.claim: So the model says Argentina, at 30.8%, is the team to beat — and history is unkind to favourites. Only eight nations have ever won a men's World Cup, and just three of them — Brazil (5), Italy (4) and Germany (4) — hold 13 of the 22 titles (59%). Six repeat champions account for 20 of 22 (91%). Even home advantage has converted only about 27% of the time (six host winners in twenty-two). Read against a long-run favourite hit-rate of ~23%, Argentina's 30.8% sits about eight points above the bar: a slightly-stronger-than-usual favourite, not a lock.
ana_histbase.code:
import collections
# The 22 men's World Cups 1930-2022 (historical_wc_summary.csv): (year, champion-label, host).
# Self-contained: the champion + host columns are inlined verbatim; everything below is recomputed.
WC = [
    [1930,"Uruguay","Uruguay"],[1934,"Italy","Italy"],[1938,"Italy","France"],
    [1950,"Uruguay","Brazil"],[1954,"West Germany","Switzerland"],[1958,"Brazil","Sweden"],
    [1962,"Brazil","Chile"],[1966,"England","England"],[1970,"Brazil","Mexico"],
    [1974,"West Germany","West Germany"],[1978,"Argentina","Argentina"],[1982,"Italy","Spain"],
    [1986,"Argentina","Mexico"],[1990,"West Germany","Italy"],[1994,"Brazil","United States"],
    [1998,"France","France"],[2002,"Brazil","South Korea/Japan"],[2006,"Italy","Germany"],
    [2010,"Spain","South Africa"],[2014,"Germany","Brazil"],[2018,"France","Russia"],
    [2022,"Argentina","Qatar"],
]
ALIAS = {"West Germany": "Germany"}   # same nation; merge is an explicit editorial call
n = len(WC)
labels = [r[1] for r in WC]
label_counts = collections.Counter(labels)
nation_counts = collections.Counter(ALIAS.get(c, c) for c in labels)
top3 = nation_counts.most_common(3)
top3_titles = sum(v for _, v in top3)
repeat = {k: v for k, v in nation_counts.items() if v >= 2}
repeat_titles = sum(repeat.values())
host_wins = [r for r in WC if r[2] == r[1]]

print(f"Men's World Cups in table: {n} ({WC[0][0]}-{WC[-1][0]})")
print(f"Distinct champion LABELS: {len(label_counts)}  ->  merged NATIONS: {len(nation_counts)} (West Germany = Germany)")
print(f"Top-3 nations hold {top3_titles}/{n} = {100*top3_titles/n:.1f}% of titles: {[(k,v) for k,v in top3]}")
print(f"Repeat champions (>=2): {len(repeat)} nations hold {repeat_titles}/{n} = {100*repeat_titles/n:.1f}%")
print(f"Host-nation wins: {len(host_wins)}/{n} = {100*len(host_wins)/n:.1f}%")
print(f"Model's Argentina 30.8% vs cited ~23% favourite hit-rate -> +{30.8-23:.1f} pp above the long-run favourite")

ana_shootouts.title: Penalty shootouts are a coin flip — even for the favourite
ana_shootouts.claim: The model's analytic shortcut for knockout ties is forgivable because penalties are close to a coin toss. Across 678 international shootouts (1967-2026) the higher pre-match-Elo team — the favourite by the same Elo used everywhere else — won just 53.7% (two-sided binomial p=0.06 vs 50%), even though those favourites averaged a 114-point Elo edge worth about a 66% win rate in normal play. Tighten to the most lopsided ties (Elo gap >=150) and the favourite still wins only 55.7%. The team shooting first wins 53.1% of the 256 shootouts with a recorded first kicker — and at the World Cup finals specifically, just 17 of 35 (48.6%).
ana_shootouts.code:
import math
# Penalty-shootout predictability (678 international shootouts 1967-2026; shootouts.csv).
# The leak-free pre-match-Elo favourite for each shootout is computed by build_shootouts.py
# (the full job; see full_ref). Here each cut's (won, n) count + its regulation-win expectation
# are inlined; the cell recomputes the win %, a 95% Wilson CI and a two-sided binomial p-value
# vs a 50/50 coin flip using the stdlib only (no scipy).
def wilson_ci(k, nn, z=1.959963984540054):
    if nn == 0: return (0.0, 0.0)
    p = k / nn
    d = 1 + z*z/nn
    c = (p + z*z/(2*nn)) / d
    h = (z * math.sqrt(p*(1-p)/nn + z*z/(4*nn*nn))) / d
    return (100*(c-h), 100*(c+h))
def binom_two_sided_p(k, nn, p=0.5):
    from math import comb
    def pmf(i): return comb(nn, i) * p**i * (1-p)**(nn-i)
    obs = pmf(k)
    return min(1.0, sum(pmf(i) for i in range(nn+1) if pmf(i) <= obs + 1e-12))

# favourite (higher pre-match Elo) wins, by minimum Elo gap: (gap_label, won, n, expected_regulation_pct)
fav_by_gap = [("any (>=0)", 364, 678, 65.8), (">=25", 306, 565, 68.4),
              (">=50", 252, 473, 70.7), (">=100", 169, 321, 75.0), (">=150", 112, 201, 79.1)]
first_shooter = (136, 256)     # team taking the first kick wins
wc_first = (17, 35)            # World Cup finals subset

print("Favourite (higher pre-match Elo) wins the shootout, by Elo gap:")
for lab, k, nn, exp in fav_by_gap:
    lo, hi = wilson_ci(k, nn)
    print(f"  gap {lab:9} n={nn:>3}  fav wins {100*k/nn:4.1f}% (95% CI {lo:.1f}-{hi:.1f})  vs {exp:.1f}% expected in regulation")
k, nn = fav_by_gap[0][1], fav_by_gap[0][2]
print(f"Headline: across {nn} shootouts the better team won {100*k/nn:.1f}% "
      f"(two-sided binomial p={binom_two_sided_p(k, nn):.3f} vs 50%) - barely above a coin flip.")
fk, fn = first_shooter
print(f"First shooter wins {100*fk/fn:.1f}% of {fn} shootouts with a recorded first kicker.")
wk, wn = wc_first
print(f"At the World Cup finals, the first shooter has won just {wk} of {wn} ({100*wk/wn:.1f}%).")

det_favbase.title: How often does the favourite actually win? ~23%
det_favbase.claim: Pre-tournament favourites have won only about 23% of men's World Cups: by FIFA's review of the previous 22 men's tournaments, the listed favourite has lifted the trophy only five times. Since 1966, when pre-tournament odds were first recorded, the shortest-priced favourite went on to win just three times — West Germany 1974, Brazil 1994 and Spain 2010. This is the external anchor the page reads the model's 30.8% against: 30.8% sits about eight points above the long-run favourite hit-rate, so the model is calling Argentina a slightly-stronger-than-usual favourite, not a certainty.

des_shootout_evaporate_chart.title: When penalties decide it, the favourite's edge nearly vanishes (line)
des_shootout_evaporate_chart.claim: The model's analytic shortcut for knockout ties is forgivable because penalties are close to a coin toss. Across 678 international shootouts (1967-2026) the higher pre-match-Elo team — the favourite by the same Elo used everywhere else — won just 53.7% (two-sided binomial p=0.06 vs 50%), even though those favourites averaged a 114-point Elo edge worth about a 66% win rate in normal play. Tighten to the most lopsided ties (Elo gap >=150) and the favourite still wins only 55.7%. The team shooting first wins 53.1% of the 256 shootouts with a recorded first kicker — and at the World Cup finals specifically, just 17 of 35 (48.6%).
des_shootout_evaporate_chart.code:
import math
# Penalty-shootout predictability (678 international shootouts 1967-2026; shootouts.csv).
# The leak-free pre-match-Elo favourite for each shootout is computed by build_shootouts.py
# (the full job; see full_ref). Here each cut's (won, n) count + its regulation-win expectation
# are inlined; the cell recomputes the win %, a 95% Wilson CI and a two-sided binomial p-value
# vs a 50/50 coin flip using the stdlib only (no scipy).
def wilson_ci(k, nn, z=1.959963984540054):
    if nn == 0: return (0.0, 0.0)
    p = k / nn
    d = 1 + z*z/nn
    c = (p + z*z/(2*nn)) / d
    h = (z * math.sqrt(p*(1-p)/nn + z*z/(4*nn*nn))) / d
    return (100*(c-h), 100*(c+h))
def binom_two_sided_p(k, nn, p=0.5):
    from math import comb
    def pmf(i): return comb(nn, i) * p**i * (1-p)**(nn-i)
    obs = pmf(k)
    return min(1.0, sum(pmf(i) for i in range(nn+1) if pmf(i) <= obs + 1e-12))

# favourite (higher pre-match Elo) wins, by minimum Elo gap: (gap_label, won, n, expected_regulation_pct)
fav_by_gap = [("any (>=0)", 364, 678, 65.8), (">=25", 306, 565, 68.4),
              (">=50", 252, 473, 70.7), (">=100", 169, 321, 75.0), (">=150", 112, 201, 79.1)]
first_shooter = (136, 256)     # team taking the first kick wins
wc_first = (17, 35)            # World Cup finals subset

print("Favourite (higher pre-match Elo) wins the shootout, by Elo gap:")
for lab, k, nn, exp in fav_by_gap:
    lo, hi = wilson_ci(k, nn)
    print(f"  gap {lab:9} n={nn:>3}  fav wins {100*k/nn:4.1f}% (95% CI {lo:.1f}-{hi:.1f})  vs {exp:.1f}% expected in regulation")
k, nn = fav_by_gap[0][1], fav_by_gap[0][2]
print(f"Headline: across {nn} shootouts the better team won {100*k/nn:.1f}% "
      f"(two-sided binomial p={binom_two_sided_p(k, nn):.3f} vs 50%) - barely above a coin flip.")
fk, fn = first_shooter
print(f"First shooter wins {100*fk/fn:.1f}% of {fn} shootouts with a recorded first kicker.")
wk, wn = wc_first
print(f"At the World Cup finals, the first shooter has won just {wk} of {wn} ({100*wk/wn:.1f}%).")
